messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Authority Presence: Police, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Mehta is a 41-year-old South Asian American graphic designer who lives with his wife in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. He came to the clinic after more than a year of what he described, haltingly, as "not being able to get back to normal." He struggled to say much more than that in the first session, not because he lacked intelligence or willingness, but because whenever he tried to recount what had happened, the thread of the story seemed to dissolve before he could finish a sentence. He would begin, pause, look at his hands, and say only that it was "complicated" — that he knew what had happened, he simply could not seem to find the words to make it land.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Rajan was detained by police following what he later learned was a tip provided by a colleague — someone he had considered a close friend, a man he had mentored and trusted for several years at the small design studio where he worked. The tip alleged, falsely, that Rajan had been involved in financial misconduct at the firm. Officers arrived at his home on a weekday morning. He remembers the smell most vividly: something acrid and burnt, which he later understood came from a flare or device used during the initial approach to his property. That smell embedded itself in the encounter with a precision that nothing else has matched. He was handcuffed in his front doorway while his wife watched from the hallway. He was held for several hours, questioned, and ultimately released without charge. No formal apology was issued. The colleague who had made the report was never disciplined.

In the weeks that followed, Rajan found himself replaying the morning with an intensity that felt less like memory and more like re-entry. When he tries to recall the event, what rises most immediately is not fear but guilt — a grinding, sourceless guilt that he has not been able to explain or argue himself out of. He had come to believe, somewhere beneath rational thought, that a person who was truly innocent would not have been treated that way. This belief has not left him.

He began noticing, gradually, that certain things in his daily environment had become unbearable. The burnt smell from a colleague's lunch in the break room microwave, or from a candle in a nearby shop, would stop him cold. He began routing his commute to avoid the stretch of road where a police substation sits, and on the occasions when he encounters an officer or a security guard — anyone in uniform — he feels his body reorganize itself around vigilance, scanning for intention, for danger, for the moment things might turn. He had come to believe that the world contains threats he simply had not been alert enough to see before, and that most people, given the right circumstances, would not protect him.

The rehearsing began quietly. Before any workplace meeting, before calling his bank, before speaking to a landlord or a contractor, Rajan would spend considerable time mentally scripting what he would say, anticipating every turn the conversation might take, preparing for the moment authority might assert itself. At the design studio, this has meant that what used to be easy creative collaboration has become effortful and slow. He has missed two client pitches by over-preparing to the point of paralysis, and his manager has noted the change in his output without knowing why.

He stopped making plans. Not dramatically, not all at once, but steadily — holidays that were never booked, a home renovation left unscheduled, a conversation with his wife about starting a family that has simply not been resumed. The future had come to feel like a space he could not trust, because he had once trusted it and had been wrong.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife. She told him, quietly and without accusation, that she felt she had lost him — that she was living with someone who was present in body but absent in some essential way. Rajan said he was afraid that she was right. What he hopes for, he said at the end of the intake, is to feel like a person who can be known again — not just managed, not just survived around, but actually known.
